vf[0]: The monitor shows **ventricular fibrillation (VF)**: a shockable rhythm. What first?
[RIGHT] Shock now (defibrillate), then straight back to CPR -> VF or pulseless VT is shockable: shock as soon as the pads are on, then straight back to 2 minutes of CPR.
Epinephrine 1 mg first, then shock -> In VF the shock comes first. Epinephrine goes in after the second shock.
Stop CPR and feel for a pulse for a full minute -> A pulse check takes under 10 seconds. Every pause stops blood flow to the brain.
Synchronized cardioversion -> Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS to time the shock to. VF has none: defibrillate (an unsynchronized shock).
vf[1]: Two minutes of CPR. Rhythm check: **still VF**.
[RIGHT] Shock again, then epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3 to 5 minutes -> Still shockable: shock every time, then epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes.
Amiodarone instead of a second shock -> Shock every time the rhythm is shockable. Drugs support the shocks; they don't replace them.
Stop compressions to intubate -> Keep compressions going. A bag-mask works; a tube can go in without stopping CPR.
Sodium bicarbonate, as in every arrest -> Bicarbonate is for specific causes (high potassium, some overdoses), not every arrest.
vf[2]: Two more minutes. **Still VF** after two shocks and epinephrine.
[RIGHT] Shock, then amiodarone 300 mg IV -> VF that won't stop after shocks: amiodarone (lidocaine is the other choice). Keep shocking every 2 minutes.
Adenosine 6 mg rapid push -> Adenosine is for SVT in a patient with a pulse.
Call the code: it has been 4 minutes -> Far too early to stop. VF is the rhythm most likely to come back.
Atropine 1 mg IV -> Atropine is for a slow heart with a pulse. It was taken out of the cardiac arrest algorithm in 2010.
pea[0]: The monitor shows **a rhythm but no pulse (PEA)**: not shockable. What first?
[RIGHT] Keep CPR going; epinephrine 1 mg IV now -> Not shockable: CPR, and epinephrine as soon as possible, then every 3 to 5 minutes.
Shock it -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
Atropine 1 mg IV -> Atropine is for a slow heart with a pulse. It was taken out of the cardiac arrest algorithm in 2010.
Wait for respiratory therapy before compressions -> Compressions start now, with whoever is in the room.
pea[1]: Two minutes later, **still no pulse**. What are you hunting for?

[RIGHT] The reversible causes: the H's and T's -> Not shockable: the way back is the cause. Hunt the H's and T's: low volume, low oxygen, acid, potassium, cold, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, clot.
Nothing: keep repeating epinephrine -> Repeating epinephrine without looking for the cause rarely ends well.
A shock every 2 minutes in case it turns to VF -> Only shock a shockable rhythm. Check it every 2 minutes.
Amiodarone 300 mg -> Amiodarone is for VF and pulseless VT, not PEA or asystole.

cause:trap: Severe asthma: the chest is **stiff and over-full**, and each breath gets harder.

[RIGHT] Pause the bagging, press on the chest to let the trapped air out, then slow breaths; check for a tension pneumothorax -> In an asthma arrest, air gets trapped: breathe slowly, let it out (disconnect, press on the chest), and think of a tension pneumothorax on either side.
Bag faster and harder -> Faster, harder breaths trap more air and drop the pressure further.
A double dose of epinephrine -> A bigger dose of epinephrine doesn't help. Fix the airway.
Shock it -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
